description: A comprehensive study of organizing, managing, and storing data efficiently in memory, encompassing linear structures, hierarchical non-linear structures, and techniques for fast data retrieval.

sections.title: Arrays and Linked Lists
sections.description: Fundamental linear data structures representing contiguous and non-contiguous memory allocations respectively.

key_concepts.explanation: Arrays allocate memory in a contiguous block, allowing O(1) random access but making resizing expensive. Linked Lists allocate nodes dynamically in non-contiguous memory, connected via pointers, allowing O(1) insertion/deletion if the pointer location is known.
Singly Linked List (forward traversal only), Doubly Linked List (forward and backward traversal using two pointers per node), and Circular Linked List (last node points back to the first node).

cases.condition: Time Complexity: Array vs. Linked List
results: Accessing an element by index: Array is O(1), Linked List is O(n).
Insertion/Deletion at the beginning: Array is O(n) due to shifting, Linked List is O(1).
Insertion/Deletion at the end: Array is O(1) if capacity allows, Singly Linked List is O(n) unless a tail pointer is maintained.

sections.title: Stacks and Queues
sections.description: Abstract Data Types (ADTs) operating on strict linear insertion and deletion principles.

key_concepts.explanation: Last-In-First-Out structure. Key operations are Push (insert) and Pop (remove) at the 'top'. Used in recursion, expression evaluation, and undo mechanisms.
First-In-First-Out structure. Key operations are Enqueue (insert at 'rear') and Dequeue (remove from 'front'). Used in CPU scheduling and breadth-first search.

results: Circular Queue: Connects the last position back to the first to efficiently utilize wasted array space.
Priority Queue: Elements are dequeued based on priority rather than arrival order. Usually implemented using Heaps.
Deque (Double Ended Queue): Allows insertion and deletion at both the front and rear ends.
Stacks are utilized to convert human-readable Infix expressions (e.g., A + B) into machine-readable Postfix (A B +) or Prefix (+ A B) notation, and to evaluate them.

sections.title: Trees and Binary Search Trees (BST)
sections.description: Hierarchical non-linear data structures consisting of nodes connected by edges, optimized for searching and sorting operations.

equations: Maximum number of nodes at level 'l': 2^l (where root is at level 0)
Maximum number of nodes in a tree of height 'h': (2^(h+1)) - 1

key_concepts.explanation: For any given node, all values in its left subtree must be strictly lesser, and all values in its right subtree must be strictly greater. In-order traversal of a BST yields elements in sorted, ascending order.

Self-balancing BSTs that maintain their height close to O(log n) to prevent the worst-case scenario of degrading into a skewed tree (O(n) time complexity). They use rotations during insertion and deletion to maintain balance.

steps.title: Tree Traversals (Depth-First)
steps.detail: In-order (Left, Root, Right); Pre-order (Root, Left, Right); Post-order (Left, Right, Root).

sections.title: Graphs
sections.description: Non-linear data structures representing networks, consisting of a finite set of vertices (nodes) and a set of edges connecting them.

key_concepts.explanation: Adjacency Matrix (a 2D array, space complexity O(V^2), good for dense graphs) vs. Adjacency List (an array of linked lists, space complexity O(V + E), ideal for sparse graphs).

results: Breadth-First Search (BFS): Explores the graph level by level, radiating outward from the source. Implemented using a Queue. Excellent for finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
Depth-First Search (DFS): Explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. Implemented using a Stack (or recursion). Used for topological sorting and detecting cycles.

sections.title: Hashing
sections.description: A technique designed to provide O(1) average time complexity for insert, search, and delete operations by mapping keys directly to array indices.

key_concepts.explanation: A hash function calculates an index for a given key. A collision occurs when two distinct keys hash to the exact same index. Good hash functions distribute keys uniformly to minimize collisions.

results: Separate Chaining: Each array index holds a pointer to a linked list of entries that hashed to that same index.
Open Addressing (Linear Probing): If a collision occurs, the algorithm searches sequentially for the next available empty slot in the array.
Open Addressing (Quadratic Probing): Searches for an empty slot using a quadratic function (e.g., +1^2, +2^2, +3^2) to avoid primary clustering.
